title: Single responsibility and Open/closed
scopeHtml: Scope: why SOLID exists, SRP, OCP, strategy/enum/sealed as extension tools, and spotting violations fast.

notes.title: Why SOLID exists
notes.html:
SOLID is five habits that keep code easy to change. Software is not written once; it is edited for years. Code that is hard to change makes every new feature slow and every bug risky. SOLID (S, O, L, I, D) is a checklist for avoiding that.

The mechanism: bad design makes one change ripple into many files. Good design makes a change land in one place. You measure it by "how many files do I touch for this feature?".

Worked example. A checkout class that validates, prices, charges the card, sends email and writes logs. Changing the email provider means editing, re-testing and re-releasing the whole checkout. In a team of 6 with 3 releases a week, a 20% regression chance per touched risky file adds up to a broken release almost every month.

Industry examples. Android's own framework moved from fat Activity classes to ViewModel, Repository and UseCase layers (Google's architecture guide) for exactly this reason. Netflix and Uber split services by one responsibility so teams deploy independently.

Decision gravity. SOLID is a guide, not a law. Applying it early on a 200-line app is over-engineering. Splitting is reversible (merge classes back); a wrong abstraction used by 40 callers is a one-way door in practice.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen where one person cooks, washes, takes orders and does accounts: any change to one job disturbs all. A restaurant with roles lets you swap the dishwasher without touching the chef.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the five names with no example. Always give a before and after.
  • Saying "always apply SOLID". Seniors say when NOT to.
  • Confusing SOLID (class design) with design patterns (recipes).

notes.title: Single Responsibility Principle
notes.html:
A class should have one reason to change. Not "does one thing" but "answers to one stakeholder or concern". If finance and marketing can each force you to edit the same class, it has two responsibilities.

How to spot it: the class name needs "and" or "Manager"; it imports Android UI, JSON and SQL together; unit tests need 6 mocks.

// BEFORE: three reasons to change (format, storage, delivery)
class InvoiceService {
    String render(Order o) { return "Invoice #" + o.id + " total " + o.total; }
    void save(Order o)     { /* JDBC insert */ }
    void email(Order o)    { /* SMTP send */ }
}

// AFTER: one reason each
class InvoiceRenderer { String render(Order o) { return "Invoice #" + o.id + " total " + o.total; } }
interface InvoiceStore  { void save(Order o); }
interface InvoiceSender { void send(String to, String body); }

class InvoiceService {
    private final InvoiceRenderer renderer; private final InvoiceStore store; private final InvoiceSender sender;
    InvoiceService(InvoiceRenderer r, InvoiceStore s, InvoiceSender m) { renderer = r; store = s; sender = m; }
    void process(Order o) { store.save(o); sender.send(o.email, renderer.render(o)); }
}
class InvoiceService(
    private val renderer: InvoiceRenderer,
    private val store: InvoiceStore,
    private val sender: InvoiceSender,
) {
    fun process(o: Order) { store.save(o); sender.send(o.email, renderer.render(o)) }
}
Before                       After
+----------------+           +----------------+     +-----------------+
| InvoiceService |           | InvoiceService |---->| InvoiceRenderer |
| render()       |           | process()      |---->| InvoiceStore    |
| save()         |           +----------------+---->| InvoiceSender   |
| email()        |                                  +-----------------+
+----------------+

Worked example. Tests: before, testing render needed a DB and SMTP stub (about 80 ms and flaky). After, InvoiceRenderer is a pure function tested in under 1 ms with 5 plain asserts.

Android example. An Activity doing network, parsing, caching and UI is the classic SRP violation. Split into ViewModel (state), Repository (data), Retrofit service (network), Activity (render only).

Everyday analogy. A Swiss army knife is handy but you do not perform surgery with it. Specialist tools can be improved one at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-splitting into 50 one-method classes ("class explosion"). Responsibility is about reasons to change, not method count.
  • Saying a class must have one method.
  • Missing that a God class often grows because "it is easier to add here".

notes.title: Open/Closed Principle
notes.html:
Code should be open for extension and closed for modification. Adding a new behaviour should mean adding new code, not editing tested old code.

The mechanism is polymorphism: depend on an interface, add a new implementation. The classic smell is an if/else or when on a type that grows with every feature.

// BEFORE: every new discount edits this method
double discount(String type, double amt) {
    if (type.equals("STUDENT")) return amt * 0.10;
    if (type.equals("VIP"))     return amt * 0.20;
    return 0;
}

// AFTER: add a class, edit nothing
interface DiscountPolicy { double apply(double amt); }
class StudentDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { public double apply(double a) { return a * 0.10; } }
class VipDiscount     implements DiscountPolicy { public double apply(double a) { return a * 0.20; } }
class BlackFridayDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { public double apply(double a) { return a * 0.40; } }
fun interface DiscountPolicy { fun apply(amt: Double): Double }
val student = DiscountPolicy { it * 0.10 }
val blackFriday = DiscountPolicy { it * 0.40 }   // new feature, no old code touched

Worked example. An e-commerce app with 12 discount types in one when. A new rule touches the shared method, so all 12 need regression tests (12 cases). With policies, a new rule is 1 class and 1 test, and the other 11 cannot break.

Industry examples. Java's Comparator, Collections.sort(list, cmp) never changes when you add a new ordering. Android RecyclerView.Adapter and Retrofit Converter.Factory and OkHttp Interceptor chain are extension points. Spring and Dagger bind implementations without editing callers.

Decision gravity. Choose the extension seam where change is likely (discounts, payment methods, notification channels), not everywhere. Wrong seam guessed = dead abstraction nobody uses; adding an interface later is easy and reversible, so wait for the second case ("rule of three").

When it breaks. Prediction fails: a requirement cuts across all policies (for example "stack discounts") and the interface must change anyway, which touches every implementation.

Everyday analogy. A power strip: you plug new devices in without rewiring the wall.

Common interview traps.

  • Closed does not mean "never edit a file ever"; bug fixes are fine.
  • Premature interfaces for things that will never vary.
  • if (x instanceof ...) chains defeat OCP; name this smell.

notes.title: Strategy, enums and sealed types as OCP tools
notes.html:
Three ways to get open/closed, from most to least open.

  1. Interface plus implementations (Strategy). Open to third parties; new types can live in other modules.
  2. Enum with behaviour. Closed set, compiler knows all cases, easy to read.
  3. Sealed type with when. Closed hierarchy; adding a case forces every when to be updated (compiler error), which is "closed for silent breakage".
enum Shipping {
    STANDARD { double cost(double kg) { return 40 + kg * 10; } },
    EXPRESS  { double cost(double kg) { return 120 + kg * 25; } };
    abstract double cost(double kg);
}
sealed interface Payment
data class Card(val last4: String) : Payment
data class Upi(val vpa: String) : Payment
// adding Wallet breaks every exhaustive when -> compiler lists places to fix
fun fee(p: Payment) = when (p) { is Card -> 2.0; is Upi -> 0.0 }

Worked example. Shipping with 2 modes: 1 enum, 6 lines. If a partner must plug in "DroneDelivery" from their own jar, you need the interface; enum cannot do that.

Decision gravity. Open set (plugins, SDKs) -> interface. Closed domain set (payment kinds you own) -> sealed, because you WANT the compiler to flag unhandled cases. Switching later is a moderate refactor.

Everyday analogy. A vending machine with fixed slots (enum) versus a food court where any stall can join (interface).

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming sealed types violate OCP; they trade extensibility for exhaustiveness on purpose.
  • Forgetting Java sealed needs Java 17; Kotlin sealed is older.

notes.title: Spotting violations quickly
notes.html:
Fast checklist for interviews. Say these out loud while reviewing code.

Smell                              Principle     Fix
-------------------------------    ----------    ---------------------------
Class name "XManager/Helper/Util"  SRP           split by reason to change
Method > ~30 lines, 3 concerns     SRP           extract class / method
switch on type grows each sprint   OCP           polymorphism / strategy
instanceof chains                  OCP           virtual method / visitor
Shotgun surgery (1 change, 8 files) SRP/OCP      group what changes together
Divergent change (1 class, many reasons) SRP     split

Worked example refactor. A ReportGenerator with generatePdf, generateCsv, email, and queryDb. Step 1: extract ReportData loader. Step 2: ReportFormat interface with Pdf and Csv. Step 3: ReportSender. Result: adding Excel is one new class; the PDF code stays untouched and untouched means no regression retest.

Everyday analogy. Tidying a garage: group by purpose, so finding or replacing a tool does not mean emptying the whole room.

Common interview traps.

  • Refactoring with no tests. State that you add characterization tests first.
  • Big-bang rewrite instead of small steps; each step must compile and pass.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• SOLID keeps change local; apply it where change is likely, not everywhere.
  • SRP: one reason to change (one stakeholder/concern), not one method.
  • OCP: add new code instead of editing old; use an interface seam at the point of variation.
  • Open set -> interface/strategy; closed set -> enum or sealed type with exhaustive when.
  • Smells: God class, growing when/if, instanceof chains, shotgun surgery.
  • Avoid class explosion and premature abstraction; wait for the second or third real case.

questions.promptHtml: What is SOLID and why should a developer care about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand the goal (cheap change) or only memorised five letters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SOLID is five design habits (Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion) whose one goal is that a change lands in one place. Code is edited for years, so the real cost is how many files I touch and re-test per feature. It is a guide, not a law: on a 200-line app it is over-engineering.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Bad design makes a change ripple: new requirement, tangled class, edit 8 files, regression. Good design keeps it local. The metric I use is "files touched per feature". If 20% of risky files regress per release and I touch 5 of them with 3 releases a week, a broken release roughly every month is expected, not bad luck.

Tangled:  requirement -> Checkout(validate+price+charge+email+log) -> edit, retest everything
Split:    requirement -> EmailSender only                         -> edit, retest 1 class

SOLID is about class design; design patterns are recipes that often implement it (Strategy implements OCP).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reciting five names with no before/after code.
  • Saying "always apply SOLID"; seniors say when NOT to.
  • Confusing SOLID with design patterns.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure whether a design is good? -> Files touched and tests re-run per typical feature.
  2. When would you skip SOLID? -> Throwaway scripts, tiny apps, stable code that never varies.
  3. Is splitting classes reversible? -> Yes, merging back is easy; a wrong abstraction with 40 callers is a one-way door in practice.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the letters. Senior ties each to change cost, names the cost of applying it (indirection, more files) and says apply at points of likely variation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 2,000-line CheckoutService made every email-provider change a full regression cycle until it was split by reason to change.

questions.promptHtml: What does the Single Responsibility Principle actually say? Does it mean a class should have only one method?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The popular misreading ("does one thing") is a common trap; they want the "reason to change" reading.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SRP says a class should have one reason to change, meaning it answers to one stakeholder or concern. It does not mean one method. If finance and marketing can each force me to edit the same class, it has two responsibilities.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Smells: the class name needs "and" or ends in Manager/Helper, it imports UI, JSON and SQL together, or unit tests need 6 mocks. Take InvoiceService with render, save, email: format, storage and delivery change for different reasons.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class InvoiceService {
    private final InvoiceRenderer renderer; private final InvoiceStore store; private final InvoiceSender sender;
    InvoiceService(InvoiceRenderer r, InvoiceStore s, InvoiceSender m) { renderer = r; store = s; sender = m; }
    void process(Order o) { store.save(o); sender.send(o.email, renderer.render(o)); }
}
class InvoiceService(

}

Side effect: InvoiceRenderer becomes a pure function, tested in under 1 ms versus about 80 ms with a DB and SMTP stub.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Over-splitting into 50 one-method classes ("class explosion").
  • Equating responsibility with method count.
  • Not noticing a God class grows because "it is easier to add here".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you spot a violation in review? -> "And" in the name, mixed imports, many mocks in tests.
  2. Android example? -> Activity doing network, parsing, cache and UI; split into ViewModel, Repository, service.
  3. Where do you stop splitting? -> When the pieces no longer change for different reasons.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "one class one job". Senior says "one reason to change per actor" and warns about class explosion.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An Activity with 1,800 lines could not be unit tested; each bug fix broke two other screens.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the Open/Closed Principle with a concrete example. Does "closed" mean you can never edit a file?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can show polymorphism replacing a growing if/else, and know the limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Open for extension, closed for modification: adding behaviour should mean adding new code, not editing tested code. I depend on an interface and add an implementation. Closed does not forbid bug fixes; it targets the if/else on type that grows with every feature.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Before: discount(String type, double amt) with an if per type, so each new rule edits a shared method and all 12 existing cases need re-testing. After: one DiscountPolicy interface; a new rule is 1 class and 1 test, and the other 11 cannot break.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface DiscountPolicy { double apply(double amt); }
class StudentDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { public double apply(double a) { return a * 0.10; } }
class BlackFridayDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { public double apply(double a) { return a * 0.40; } }
fun interface DiscountPolicy { fun apply(amt: Double): Double }
val blackFriday = DiscountPolicy { it * 0.40 }   // new feature, no old code touched

JDK analogy: Collections.sort(list, cmp) never changes when a new ordering appears.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Interfaces for things that will never vary (premature abstraction).
  • instanceof chains that quietly defeat OCP.
  • Guessing the wrong seam; wait for the second or third real case.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does OCP fail? -> A cross-cutting requirement like "stack discounts" forces the interface to change and every implementation with it.
  2. Which seam do you pick? -> Where change is likely: discounts, payment methods, notification channels.
  3. How is it tested? -> Each policy tested alone; the core tested with a fake policy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the Shape example. Senior picks the seam by likelihood of change, uses the rule of three and admits prediction can fail.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 12-branch when for discounts regressed on every campaign until it became policy classes.

questions.promptHtml: You need to vary behaviour by payment type. When do you choose an interface, an enum with behaviour, or a sealed type?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who know "open set vs closed set" from those who default to an interface always.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Open set that third parties may extend: interface/Strategy. Closed set I own, where I want the compiler to know every case: enum with behaviour. Closed hierarchy with different data per case: sealed type plus exhaustive when, so adding a case becomes a compile error everywhere it matters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sealed types are not an OCP violation; they trade extensibility for exhaustiveness on purpose ("closed for silent breakage"). A partner plugging in "DroneDelivery" from their own jar needs an interface; an enum cannot do that. Java sealed needs Java 17; Kotlin sealed is older.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
enum Shipping {
    STANDARD { double cost(double kg) { return 40 + kg * 10; } },
    EXPRESS  { double cost(double kg) { return 120 + kg * 25; } };
    abstract double cost(double kg);
}
sealed interface Payment
data class Card(val last4: String) : Payment
data class Upi(val vpa: String) : Payment
fun fee(p: Payment) = when (p) { is Card -> 2.0; is Upi -> 0.0 }  // adding Wallet breaks this

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming sealed types violate OCP.
  • Using an enum where a plugin module must add values.
  • Forgetting the Java 17 requirement.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Switching later? -> Moderate refactor; moving enum to interface is mechanical but touches callers.
  2. Why not always an interface? -> No exhaustiveness check; silent missing cases.
  3. Where does a sealed when hurt? -> If the sealed type is in a published library, adding a case breaks all consumers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks interface always. Senior states open vs closed set and exhaustiveness as the deciding factor.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A new Wallet payment was missed in one if chain and silently charged zero fee; a sealed when would have failed the build.

questions.contextHtml:
A ReportGenerator (900 lines, 4 owners in git blame) has queryDb(), generatePdf(), generateCsv() and email(). Product wants Excel next sprint. Last quarter 3 of 5 releases touching this file caused a regression in unrelated output. There are no unit tests, only a manual QA checklist.

class ReportGenerator {
    byte[] generate(String format, int id) {
        List<Row> rows = jdbc.query("select ...", id);
        if (format.equals("pdf")) { /* 300 lines */ }
        else if (format.equals("csv")) { /* 80 lines */ }
        mailer.send(user.email, bytes);
        return bytes;
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Which smells do you see, what classes would you extract, and in what order do you refactor?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite it with design patterns." No tests first, no steps, a big-bang rewrite that cannot ship incrementally.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are PDF/CSV outputs contractually byte-stable (decides characterization tests)? Who else calls generate? Is mailing always required? Release cadence?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add characterization tests that capture current PDF and CSV output for 5 sample ids before touching anything.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (smells): Divergent change (one class, many reasons: SRP), a growing if on format (OCP), mixed IO (DB, mail) with formatting.
  4. How I'd verify: Count distinct imports (JDBC, PDF lib, SMTP), look at git blame for which concerns change together, check call sites.
  5. Root cause: "Easier to add here" growth: no seam between loading, formatting and sending.
  6. Fix (small steps, each compiles and passes): (a) extract ReportLoader; (b) ReportFormat interface with Pdf, Csv; (c) ReportSender; (d) ReportService composes them. Excel is then one new class.
  7. Prevention: Format classes tested as pure functions; a review rule "new format = new class".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang rewrite, no Visitor for two formats, no interface for the loader until a test needs a fake.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface ReportFormat { byte[] render(List<Row> rows); }
class ReportService {
    private final ReportLoader loader; private final Map<String, ReportFormat> formats; private final ReportSender sender;
    ReportService(ReportLoader l, Map<String, ReportFormat> f, ReportSender s) { loader = l; formats = f; sender = s; }
    byte[] generate(String fmt, int id) { byte[] b = formats.get(fmt).render(loader.load(id)); sender.send(b); return b; }
}
fun interface ReportFormat { fun render(rows: List<Row>): ByteArray }
class ReportService(private val loader: ReportLoader, private val formats: Map<String, ReportFormat>, private val sender: ReportSender) {
    fun generate(fmt: String, id: Int): ByteArray = formats.getValue(fmt).render(loader.load(id)).also(sender::send)
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing wants a partner to supply formats -> keep the interface, load implementations through a registry or ServiceLoader.
  • Only two formats ever? -> A plain when is fine; the seam is for Excel arriving.
  • Tests are impossible without a DB -> that is exactly why loader is extracted first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A report class that grew one method a quarter was split in four small PRs; the Excel feature then shipped in half a day and the PDF path stayed untouched.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes a rewrite or patterns by name only.
  • Hire: names SRP and OCP smells, extracts format interface, mentions tests.
  • Strong hire: characterization tests first, incremental steps, states when NOT to abstract.

questions.contextHtml: An order system computes price with a Pricing.total(order) method containing a switch (customer.tier) for REGULAR, STUDENT, VIP. Marketing now adds a Black Friday 40% rule and a coupon rule, each requested separately, and says more campaign rules arrive monthly. Team of 6, 3 deploys a week. The switch is already 90 lines and has 14 tests.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change for the Black Friday rule today, and how would you restructure so the next campaign needs no edits to old code?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add another case to the switch, it is quick." Or invents a rule engine DSL for 3 rules.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do rules stack or are they exclusive? Is order of application significant? Are campaigns time-boxed (switch on/off without deploy)? Who defines rules?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship Black Friday as one new class if time is tight, rather than another switch branch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Seam is DiscountPolicy; stacking is the likely cross-cutting requirement that could break the interface.
  4. How I'd verify: Ask product for 3 upcoming rules and test whether the interface fits all of them.
  5. Root cause: Behaviour keyed on a type string, so every variation edits the shared method.
  6. Fix: DiscountPolicy.apply(Order): Money; Pricing receives List<DiscountPolicy> by constructor. Each existing branch becomes a class with its original tests moved with it. Black Friday adds 1 class and 1 test; the 14 existing cases stay valid.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: no new branches on tier or campaign.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No rule engine for 3 rules; rule of three says the interface is now justified (3+ real cases).

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface DiscountPolicy { Money apply(Order o, Money running); }
class Pricing {
    private final List<DiscountPolicy> policies;
    Pricing(List<DiscountPolicy> p) { policies = p; }
    Money total(Order o) { Money m = o.subtotal(); for (DiscountPolicy p : policies) m = p.apply(o, m); return m; }
}
fun interface DiscountPolicy { fun apply(o: Order, running: Money): Money }
class Pricing(private val policies: List<DiscountPolicy>) {
    fun total(o: Order) = policies.fold(o.subtotal()) { m, p -> p.apply(o, m) }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Max discount capped at 50%" -> a final cap policy or a decorator; do not edit each rule.
  • Rules must be toggled without deploy -> load enabled policy list from config; interface unchanged.
  • Cap needs knowledge of all other rules -> the interface assumption broke; accept one signature change.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promo month introduced 6 rules in one if ladder; two interacted wrongly and over-discounted for 4 hours. After the policy split each rule had an isolated test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a branch.
  • Hire: policy interface injected by constructor.
  • Strong hire: asks about stacking, anticipates cross-cutting break, justifies by rule of three.

questions.contextHtml: A junior's PR for a 120-line UserRegistration flow adds 14 classes: UserNameValidator, UserEmailValidator, UserPasswordHasher, UserIdGenerator, UserSaver, UserRegistrationFacade, UserRegistrationFacadeImpl and more. Each has one method and one implementation. The PR description says "applied SRP everywhere". Build time and navigation cost went up; a one-field change now touches 5 files.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks SOLID, approve" or "too many classes, reject" with no reasoning about reasons to change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which of these change for different reasons or stakeholders? Is there a second implementation planned? Which need fakes in tests?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not block on style; ask the author to merge pieces that always change together.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Class explosion (responsibility confused with method count); Impl suffix with one implementation is noise; facade with no added value.
  4. How I'd verify: Look at git history of similar features: do validators for name and email ever change independently? Count files touched for a typical change.
  5. Root cause: SRP read as "one method per class", not "one reason to change".
  6. Fix: Keep RegistrationValidator (one reason: validation rules), PasswordHasher (security policy, needs a fake in tests), UserRepository (storage boundary) and RegistrationService. Delete the facade and the Impl layers.
  7. Prevention: Review checklist: "which stakeholder changes this?" and rule of three for interfaces.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not collapse back into one class, since hashing and storage really do change for other reasons.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Author says "we will need many validators later" -> split when the second real validator arrives, it is reversible.
  • Why keep the hasher separate? -> Security policy changes on its own schedule, and tests should not pay bcrypt cost.
  • How to coach a junior? -> Explain the rule with their own diff, not by authority.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team with 300 one-method classes needed three days to onboard anyone; merging them into 40 cohesive classes cut feature PR size in half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts or rejects without a principle.
  • Hire: names class explosion, keeps meaningful splits.
  • Strong hire: decides per class by reason-to-change evidence and coaches.

questions.contextHtml:
A notification module has this code and a bug report: "WhatsApp messages never get a retry, SMS does". The team added WhatsApp last week.

void send(Notifier n, String msg) {
    if (n instanceof SmsNotifier) { n.send(msg); retry(n, msg, 3); }
    else if (n instanceof EmailNotifier) { n.send(msg); }
    else { n.send(msg); }   // WhatsApp falls here
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong structurally, what is the immediate bug, and how do you fix it so it cannot recur?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds else if (n instanceof WhatsAppNotifier) and moves on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the retry policy per channel? Is retry safe for non-idempotent sends (duplicate messages)? Where else is instanceof Notifier used?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the missing retry for WhatsApp after confirming idempotency.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: instanceof chain (OCP smell) means each new channel can be silently missed; retry belongs to the channel's contract; shotgun surgery likely elsewhere.
  4. How I'd verify: grep instanceof across the module and list every place that branches on notifier type.
  5. Root cause: Behaviour that varies by type lives in the caller, not in the type.
  6. Fix: Move it into the type via a virtual method, or inject a retry policy.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Notifier { void send(String msg); default int maxRetries() { return 0; } }
class SmsNotifier implements Notifier { public void send(String m) { /* ... */ } public int maxRetries() { return 3; } }
void send(Notifier n, String msg) { Retry.run(n.maxRetries(), () -> n.send(msg)); }
interface Notifier { fun send(msg: String); val maxRetries: Int get() = 0 }
class SmsNotifier : Notifier { override fun send(msg: String) {}; override val maxRetries = 3 }
fun send(n: Notifier, msg: String) = Retry.run(n.maxRetries) { n.send(msg) }
  1. Prevention: A test that iterates all Notifier implementations and checks the retry contract; lint ban on instanceof of own hierarchy.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Visitor for 3 types; default method is enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retries risk duplicate WhatsApp messages -> need idempotency keys; retry only on timeouts known safe.
  • Closed set of channels and you want compile errors -> sealed type with when.
  • Third-party channels from plugins -> interface, not sealed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A missed branch for a new payment method silently used the default fee of zero for a week; a polymorphic method would have forced the decision.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds another else if.
  • Hire: moves behaviour into the type.
  • Strong hire: also greps for the same smell, adds contract test, flags idempotency.

questions.contextHtml: PaymentService.pay() validates the card, calls a gateway over HTTP, writes to MySQL and sends an email. Its unit test takes 3.2 s (Testcontainers MySQL plus a WireMock server), the suite of 400 such tests takes 21 minutes in CI, and developers skip it locally. Flaky rate is 4% per run, mostly the SMTP stub.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change in the design to cut test time and flakiness, and what would you still leave as integration tests?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy a faster CI box" or "mock everything with Mockito" including internal pure logic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tests need real MySQL semantics (locking, constraints)? Does the gateway have a sandbox? Is the logic mostly branching rules?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tag slow tests and run them only on merge; keep a fast subset locally.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Pure rules mixed with IO; each test pays infrastructure cost for logic that needs none; SMTP stub flakiness from real network ports.
  4. How I'd verify: Profile the test: time spent in container start, HTTP, assertion. Count tests that really assert DB behaviour.
  5. Root cause: Several reasons to change in one class force the full stack into each test.
  6. Fix: Extract CardValidator (pure), PaymentGateway, PaymentRepository, ReceiptSender as seams; test rules with plain asserts (under 1 ms), use in-memory fakes for orchestration (about 1 ms), keep 10 integration tests for the real SQL and gateway contract.
  7. Prevention: Test pyramid target: 90% fast, under 60 s total.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not mocking the DB for SQL-semantic tests: a fake cannot prove a unique constraint.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fake and real repository diverge -> shared contract test run against both.
  • Is Mockito wrong here? -> Fine for "email sent once"; prefer fakes for state.
  • 400 tests x 1 ms = 0.4 s, so why keep integration tests? -> They catch mapping and migration bugs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 25-minute suite became 40 seconds after splitting rules from IO; coverage actually rose because people ran it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: throws hardware or blanket mocks at it.
  • Hire: splits seams and uses fakes.
  • Strong hire: keeps a thin integration layer, contract tests for fakes, quantifies.

questions.contextHtml: Six months ago the team introduced ShippingStrategy (STANDARD, EXPRESS) "for OCP". Now product asks for: free shipping above 999 for all methods, a holiday surcharge on all methods, and carrier-specific cut-off times. Each requirement forces changes to ShippingStrategy.cost() signature and all implementations; PRs touch 9 files, and the original interface has 2 implementations only.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong with the OCP application, and what do you do now?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more parameters to the interface" or "OCP is useless".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which rules are per-method and which are cross-cutting? Will new carriers be added? Is order of rule application important?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship this sprint's rule as a decorator or a post-step rather than widening the signature again.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The seam was drawn on the wrong axis (carrier choice) while the real variation is cross-cutting adjustments; prediction failed, which OCP admits can happen.
  4. How I'd verify: List the last 10 shipping changes and classify them: new method, adjustment across methods, or cut-off logic.
  5. Root cause: Abstraction chosen before real cases existed; cross-cutting changes always touch every implementation.
  6. Fix: Keep ShippingStrategy for base cost; add a chain of PriceAdjustment rules (free-above, holiday) applied by the pricing service; model cut-off in a separate Schedule type.
  7. Prevention: Rule of three before adding an interface; write the second and third requirement in the design doc before choosing the seam.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not deleting the strategy (it still fits carrier cost); not a generic rules engine yet.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PriceAdjustment { Money adjust(Order o, Money current); }
Money total(Order o) {
    Money m = strategy.cost(o);
    for (PriceAdjustment a : adjustments) m = a.adjust(o, m);
    return m;
}
fun interface PriceAdjustment { fun adjust(o: Order, current: Money): Money }
fun total(o: Order) = adjustments.fold(strategy.cost(o)) { m, a -> a.adjust(o, m) }

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Free shipping must apply before surcharge -> explicit ordering in the list, with a test.
  • Would you revert to a switch? -> Possibly, if the set truly never changes.
  • Public SDK already exposes ShippingStrategy -> one-way door; add the new interface beside it and deprecate slowly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An early interface guessed from two cases survived only one; after three real cases the correct seam looked nothing like the first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: widens the interface again.
  • Hire: separates cross-cutting adjustments.
  • Strong hire: diagnoses wrong-seam prediction, cites rule of three, considers API compatibility.

questions.contextHtml: Backend models Payment as an enum PaymentType {CARD, UPI, NETBANKING} with 11 switch statements across 7 services. Product wants to add WALLET and, next quarter, partner-provided methods from external jars. A previous addition of NETBANKING missed one switch and shipped a null fee for 2 hours (about 3,000 orders). Deploys are daily; no downtime allowed.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate so WALLET ships safely now and partner methods become possible later?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds WALLET to the enum and greps for switch.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are partners really coming (decides interface vs sealed)? Is the enum persisted as a string or ordinal in DB or messages (compatibility)? Are fees in one place?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship WALLET behind a flag after adding exhaustiveness checks so the compiler finds every use.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Switches without exhaustiveness (Java switch statement over enum has no default error) leave holes; behaviour belongs in the type; partner support needs an open set.
  4. How I'd verify: grep all 11 switches; add default -> throw temporarily to surface gaps in tests.
  5. Root cause: Behaviour per payment type is scattered; the enum carries no behaviour.
  6. Fix (staged): Step 1, make switch expressions exhaustive (compile error on missing case). Step 2, move fee() and validate() into the type (PaymentMethod interface, enum implements it). Step 3, when partners are confirmed, callers depend on the interface and the enum is one provider. Persist the string id, never ordinal.
  7. Prevention: Contract test iterating PaymentMethod providers; lint on switch over payment type.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a sealed hierarchy if partners ship jars (sealed forbids outside subclasses).

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PaymentMethod { String id(); Money fee(Money amt); }
enum BuiltIn implements PaymentMethod {
    CARD { public Money fee(Money a) { return a.pct(2); } },
    WALLET { public Money fee(Money a) { return a.pct(1); } };
    public String id() { return name(); }
}
interface PaymentMethod { val id: String; fun fee(amt: Money): Money }
enum class BuiltIn(override val id: String) : PaymentMethod {
    CARD("CARD") { override fun fee(amt: Money) = amt.pct(2) },
    WALLET("WALLET") { override fun fee(amt: Money) = amt.pct(1) }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old messages contain ordinal values -> keep a migration mapper; never reuse ordinals.
  • Fees need per-partner config -> provider returns a rate object loaded at startup.
  • Why not keep sealed for the internal set? -> Fine if no partners; exhaustiveness is valuable then.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A missed switch case sent zero-fee orders for two hours; the fix was moving fee into the type so a missing implementation could not compile.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds enum value and hopes.
  • Hire: moves behaviour into type, staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: separates open vs closed set decision, handles persistence compatibility.

questions.contextHtml: In an interview you are told: "Design the discount system for our app so it is flexible." Nothing else. You have 35 minutes. A teammate shows a 40-class design from a past project (rules engine, DSL, plugin loader) and says SOLID demands it.
questions.promptHtml: How do you approach the design, and how do you decide how much SOLID to apply?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts drawing 15 interfaces immediately or says "I will use all five principles".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which discount kinds exist now (3 or 30)? Do they stack? Who creates them: developers or business users? Expected new rules per month? Latency or audit needs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the scope in writing: assume 3 rules (student, VIP, coupon), developer-defined, no stacking, then confirm.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Variation is in rule kinds (seam: DiscountPolicy); stacking and business-user rules would change the design to a pipeline or engine.
  4. How I'd verify: Walk two new requirements ("Black Friday", "cap at 50%") through the design and count the files touched.
  5. Root cause of risk: Over-design if I guess far ahead; under-design if I hardcode a switch.
  6. Design: DiscountPolicy interface, 3 implementations, Pricing receiving a list by constructor, tests with fakes. Mention what I did not build: engine, DSL, plugin loading.
  7. Prevention: State triggers for revisiting: a 5th rule, cross-rule interaction, non-developer authors.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No DSL until a non-developer needs to author rules; the cost is more files, indirection and onboarding time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer says rules will be authored by business users -> now a rules table or DSL is justified; discuss validation and audit.
  • Rules must stack with priorities -> ordered pipeline plus conflict policy.
  • Teammate insists on the 40-class design -> ask which of the 40 has a second implementation today.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "flexible" rules engine built for 3 rules took three months and was used for 2 rules; the interface plus a list of classes would have shipped in two days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: draws everything with no questions.
  • Hire: asks scope, applies seam at the likely variation.
  • Strong hire: states what is not built and the triggers to revisit, tests the design with a changed requirement.
